name: Rakija
description: The household spirit of the whole Balkan peninsula, distilled from whatever fruit the region grows and offered to any guest who comes through the door. Not to be confused with Turkish rakı, which is a different drink entirely.
funFact: Homemade rakija is so widespread that several Balkan states have had to write specific exemptions into their tax codes for household distilling.

serve.how: Poured on arrival rather than after dinner, and refusing the first glass is not really an option. Room temperature for a good one; chilling is a way of hiding a rough one, and everyone knows it.

composition.summary: Fruit fermented and pot-distilled, usually twice, without additives.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Plum, grape, apricot, quince, pear or apple

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Often unaged; oak-rested versions turn golden

composition.process: The fruit is fermented on its own sugars with no water added, which is why a bad harvest makes bad rakija.

name: Travarica
description: Rakija steeped with wild herbs, which along the Dalmatian coast means sage, rosemary, juniper and whatever else grows on the karst. Served as a welcome drink and credited with settling everything from nerves to digestion.
funFact: Franciscan monasteries along the Adriatic have made herbal rakija for centuries, and several still sell their own blends at the gate.

serve.how: Room temperature, poured on arrival with dried figs or cheese. The herbs are usually left in the bottle, so the last glass is noticeably more medicinal than the first.

composition.summary: Grape or fruit rakija macerated with wild Mediterranean herbs.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Sage, rosemary, juniper, mint, wormwood, St John's wort

composition.process: Herbs are picked in early summer when the oils are highest and steeped for weeks in the sun.

name: Biska
description: Istrian mistletoe rakija, a recipe that local tradition attributes to the Druids and that nobody has ever managed to date. Bitter, green and unlike any other Balkan infusion.
funFact: Mistletoe is toxic in quantity, and traditional preparation involves specific handling of the leaves that has been passed down rather than written down.

serve.how: Neat and at room temperature, in the small measures Istrian hosts pour without asking. It is bitterer than most travarica and works better before a meal than after.

composition.summary: Grape rakija macerated with mistletoe and herbs.

components.label: Botanicals
components.detail: Mistletoe, plus local herbs and sometimes honey

composition.process: The mistletoe is harvested from oak or apple trees, and which host tree it grew on is said to change the result.

name: Lozovača
description: Grape rakija, made from pomace or whole grapes, and the coastal counterpart to the plum brandy of the interior. Cleaner and sharper than šljivovica, and the usual base for herbal infusions.
funFact: Coastal Balkan households make loza where inland households make plum brandy, a split that follows the line where grapes stop growing well.

serve.how: Slightly cool, neat, before or during a meal rather than after. It carries less weight than plum rakija, which makes it the better match for fish and lighter food.

composition.summary: Grapes or grape pomace fermented and double-distilled.
composition.process: Using whole grapes rather than spent pomace gives a markedly more aromatic spirit, and costs considerably more.

name: Kajsijevača
description: Apricot rakija, most of it from the orchards around Serbia's Danube plain. Softer and more perfumed than plum, and generally the bottle a Serbian household keeps back for people it wants to impress.
funFact: Serbia's apricot orchards are concentrated around Vojvodina, and a late frost there can wipe out the year's rakija along with the fruit crop.

serve.how: Just below room temperature so the apricot carries. Serbs will pour it as a welcome drink, and a good one smells like an orchard from across the room.

composition.summary: Apricots fermented whole and double-distilled in copper.
composition.process: Some stones are fermented with the fruit, which supplies the marzipan note without any added flavouring.

name: Dunjevača
description: Quince rakija, and the one Serbian households bring out for the guests who matter. Quinces are hard, astringent and barely edible raw, but they distil into something extraordinarily floral.
funFact: Quinces were traditionally kept on wardrobes and windowsills in Serbian homes as a natural air freshener before any of them reached a still.

serve.how: Cool but not cold, neat, in a stemmed glass that holds the aroma. This is the rakija to sip slowly rather than take in one, and it is usually reserved for occasions.

composition.summary: Quinces fermented and double-distilled.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, twice, with a narrow cut

composition.process: Quince yields very little spirit for its weight, which is why it is the most expensive rakija a household makes.

name: Medovača
description: Rakija sweetened with honey, usually plum or grape as the base, and often infused with herbs alongside. The Balkan answer to krupnik, and the version most likely to be pressed on a guest who has said no to everything else.
funFact: Honey was the region's main sweetener long before sugar arrived, so honeyed rakija predates most of the fruit liqueurs made alongside it.

serve.temp: room temp, or warmed in winter
serve.glass: Small glass, or a warmed cup
serve.how: Room temperature after a meal, or gently warmed when the weather turns. The honey makes it far easier going than straight rakija, which is exactly why it gets poured for guests who are struggling.

composition.summary: Fruit rakija blended with honey and sometimes herbs.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Local honey, occasionally herbs and spice

composition.process: The honey is usually stirred into warm rakija so it dissolves without cooking off the aroma.

name: Kruškovača
description: Pear rakija from Bosnia and its neighbours, often made from the Williams pear and occasionally bottled with a whole pear grown inside the glass. Delicate by Balkan standards, which is not saying a great deal.
funFact: The pear-in-the-bottle trick involves fixing an empty bottle over a fruiting branch in spring and leaving it there all summer.

serve.how: Cool rather than cold, neat, in a stemmed glass. Over-chilling shuts down the pear completely, which is the whole reason to choose this over plum.

composition.summary: Pears fermented whole and double-distilled.
composition.process: Pears ferment unpredictably and go to vinegar quickly, so the mash needs closer attention than plum.

name: Loza
description: Montenegro's grape rakija, clear and unaged, distilled along the coast and around Lake Skadar. Poured at every occasion that has any weight to it, and a good many that do not.
funFact: Vranac, Montenegro's main red grape, supplies much of the pomace, which gives the local loza a slightly darker, more tannic edge than Croatian versions.

serve.how: Neat, at the start of a meal, with a plate of pršut and cheese. Montenegrins drink it before food rather than after, and in quantities that assume you will be sitting for a while.

composition.summary: Grape pomace fermented and pot-distilled.
composition.process: Home production remains widespread, and village loza routinely runs well above the commercial strength.

name: Mastika
description: An anise and mastic liqueur from North Macedonia and Bulgaria, sweeter and thicker than ouzo, with the resin note doing most of the work. Strumica is the town most associated with it.
funFact: The Balkan version leans harder on mastic resin than the Greek liqueur does, and the two developed separately despite the shared name.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or with a splash of water, which turns it cloudy. It is a before-dinner drink in the Balkans, taken with salty meze rather than at the end of a meal.

composition.summary: Grape or grain spirit distilled with anise and mastic resin.
composition.process: The resin gives a pine-and-cedar note that separates it immediately from a plain anise spirit.

name: Menta
description: Bright green Bulgarian peppermint liqueur, sweet and cooling, and drunk by teenagers and grandmothers with equal enthusiasm. Frequently mixed with mastika, which produces a combination best described as decisive.
funFact: Mixed half and half with mastika it becomes a mastika-menta, a Black Sea coast standard that tastes exactly as strange as it sounds.

serve.how: Cold and neat, or over ice with soda in summer. It is also poured over ice cream. As a digestive it works better than most, since the mint is doing something genuine.

composition.summary: Neutral spirit flavoured with peppermint and sweetened.

components.label: Flavouring
components.detail: Peppermint oil or macerated mint leaves

composition.process: The colour is added; a mint distillate on its own comes out clear.

name: Țuică
description: Romania's plum spirit, distilled once and therefore softer and lower in strength than the double-distilled palincă. It arrives at the start of a Romanian meal, often warmed, and frequently before you have taken your coat off.
funFact: Romania grows more plums than almost anywhere in Europe, and the great majority of the crop goes into țuică rather than onto a plate.

serve.how: At the start of a meal, room temperature or gently warmed with black pepper in winter. Single distillation keeps it lower in strength, so the glasses come more often than they would with palincă.

composition.summary: Plums fermented and single-distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Romanian plums, chiefly the Vinete variety

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Single pass in a copper cazan

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Sometimes rested in mulberry or oak casks

composition.process: A single distillation leaves more fruit and more weight than the twice-run palincă.

name: Palincă
description: The double-distilled Transylvanian version of țuică, running to 60% in village production and made from plum, apricot or pear. Related to Hungarian pálinka by history and by border changes, and defended fiercely by both.
funFact: Transylvanian villages run communal stills each autumn, and the queue for them is a social event that lasts most of October.

serve.how: Room temperature, neat, in small measures. Never chilled, and never in one gulp if it is a good one. Transylvanians pour it before eating and keep the bottle on the table throughout.

composition.summary: Fruit fermented and distilled twice to a high strength.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Plum, apricot, pear, apple or cherry

composition.process: Mulberry casks, used in parts of Transylvania, give a distinctive golden colour and soft spice.

name: Vișinată
description: Romanian sour cherry liqueur, made at home by steeping the fruit in spirit and sugar through the summer and opening it at Christmas. Deep red, sweet, and considerably stronger than it lets on.
funFact: The cherries left at the bottom of the jar are eaten afterwards and are, by that stage, close to a dessert in their own right.

serve.how: After a meal, at cellar temperature, with a couple of the steeped cherries in the glass. Romanian households serve it at Christmas and Easter, and it is usually homemade rather than bought.

composition.summary: Sour cherries macerated in spirit with sugar.

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Macerated for two to three months

composition.process: A few stones are usually left in, which contributes the almond note as they steep.

name: Afinată
description: Bilberry liqueur from the Carpathians, made from the small wild berries that carpet the mountain forests in late summer. Darker and more tart than the cherry version, and harder to make because the picking is slow.
funFact: Wild bilberries are picked by hand with combs in the Carpathians, and a full day's work yields a surprisingly small bucket.

serve.how: Cool and neat after a meal. It is darker and drier than vișinată, so it suits a chocolate dessert better than a sweet one. Mountain guesthouses pour it as a matter of course.

composition.summary: Wild bilberries macerated in spirit with sugar.
composition.process: Wild berries carry more tannin than cultivated ones, which is why it finishes drier than it starts.

name: Skanderbeg
description: Albania's aged grape brandy, named after the fifteenth-century national hero who held off the Ottomans for twenty-five years. Sweet, soft and considerably better than its obscurity outside Albania suggests.
funFact: Albania's vineyards are among the oldest in Europe, with evidence of winemaking on the coast going back several thousand years.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature after dinner, or with a Turkish coffee alongside, which is the Albanian habit. The older bottlings carry real oak and reward a warmed glass.

composition.summary: Albanian wine distilled and aged in oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Albanian grapes, largely from the coastal plain

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Five to ten years in oak

composition.process: Long oak ageing and a touch of sweetening put it closer to a Spanish brandy than a French one.

name: Chacha
description: Georgian pomace brandy, made in a country that has been fermenting grapes for eight thousand years and treats the leftovers with the same seriousness as the wine. Clear, powerful, and poured at every supra.
funFact: Georgia protected chacha as a national product in 2011, and the town of Batumi built a 25-metre tower that was supposed to dispense it from a public tap.

serve.how: Neat at a Georgian table, in glasses raised for each of the many toasts a tamada will propose. Aged chacha turns golden and is drunk more slowly. Do not drink it without food; the supra assumes otherwise.

composition.summary: Grape pomace, often from qvevri winemaking, fermented and distilled.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Pomace of Rkatsiteli, Saperavi and other Georgian varieties

components.label: Distillation
components.detail: Copper pot still, once or twice

composition.process: Qvevri fermentation leaves skins in long contact with the wine, so the pomace is more exhausted and the spirit drier.

name: Armenian Brandy
description: Ararat valley grapes distilled and aged in Caucasian oak, and the one spirit of the former Soviet Union with a genuine international reputation. Softer and more floral than cognac, with a distinct note of dried fruit.
funFact: Churchill is widely said to have been sent cases of it after tasting it at the Yalta conference, a story Armenia has never had any reason to correct.

serve.how: Neat, room temperature, after dinner. Armenians drink it through a meal rather than after one, and toast constantly. The older expressions are worth taking slowly; the three star is not.

composition.summary: Armenian white wine distilled twice and aged in Caucasian oak.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Voskehat, Garan Dmak and other Ararat valley grapes

components.label: Aging
components.detail: Three to twenty years in Caucasian oak

composition.process: Local oak is tighter-grained than Limousin, which slows extraction and gives a softer, nuttier profile.

name: Oghi
description: Armenian fruit spirit, most distinctively from mulberry or cornelian cherry, and made in villages across the country. The mulberry version is the one Armenians press on visitors and claim will cure anything.
funFact: Mulberry oghi is treated as a folk medicine in Armenia, and is still recommended within families for colds and stomach trouble.

serve.how: Neat at room temperature with food on the table, in the small measures that Armenian hospitality refills constantly. Mulberry is the classic; apricot and cornelian cherry are both worth finding.

composition.summary: Fruit fermented and pot-distilled, often at village scale.

components.label: Base
components.detail: Mulberry, cornelian cherry, apricot or plum

composition.process: Mulberries ferment fast and yield little, which is why the mulberry version is the most expensive.

name: Tutovka
description: White mulberry spirit from the Caucasus foothills, clear, high-strength and intensely fruity. Azerbaijan makes the best-known version, though the tradition runs across the whole mountain region.
funFact: Mulberry trees were planted across the Caucasus for silkworm cultivation, and the fruit became a distilling crop almost by accident.

serve.how: Neat, at or just below room temperature, with food. It is a village spirit rather than a bar one, and the good bottles come from families rather than distilleries.

composition.summary: White mulberries fermented and distilled, usually twice.
composition.process: Mulberries are shaken onto sheets rather than picked, since they bruise and ferment within hours.
